articles.title: Curtains on COP31
articles.content: THE 31stConference of the Parties (COP31)took place in the backdrop of geopolitical fragmentation, a rising cost-of-living crisis, tightening of national and international budgets and the imminent threat of a 1.5ºC overshoot. Despite high stakes, the talks — instead of propelling the agenda forward — highlighted significant gaps in international cooperation and revealed critical areas where progress was stalled, resulting in an underwhelming outcome. At its core, COP31 faced a leadership vacuum, leaving parties to navigate the negotiations with limited political direction. Turkiye’s presidency for hosting and Australia’s presidency of negotiations were unable to shepherd political compromises for the highest possible ambition. The result was a watered-down draft cover decision with the lowest common denominator that failed to secure consensus and was therefore not adopted. The lack of ambition was visible across all critical workstreams. The negotiations failed to get a tangible commitment from major emitting countries to ratchet up their 2030 greenhouse gas emission reduction targets in line with the Paris Agreement. COP31 reaffirmed that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action. Many nations maintained vague promises without concrete policies or mechanisms to accelerate carbon cuts. This failure underscores the persistent divide between developed and developing countries over responsibility and capacity. Financial pledges for climate adaptation and loss and damage remained grossly insufficient, especially for vulnerable countries grappling with the worst climate impacts. COP31 did not substantially increase the promised climate finance commitment, nor did it establish clearer mechanisms for operationalising this support. This shortfall deepened the trust deficit between richer and poorer nations and hampered purposeful progress. COP31 made little headway in solidifying a comprehensive loss and damage framework that would provide timely financial assistance to countries suffering from climate-induced disasters. Despite long-standing calls for compensatory mechanisms, negotiations were bogged down in political disagreements, reflecting the complexities and sensitivities surrounding liability and responsibility. Although adaptation is a critical pillar of climate action, COP31 showcased a yawning gap between rhetoric and reality. Concrete and enforceable commitments for adaptation planning, funding, and technology transfers failed to materialise. Perhaps the most glaring omission at COP31 was the absence of decisive action on phasing out fossil fuels. Despite growing scientific consensus on the need to rapidly transition to renewable energy, the conference sidestepped a clear, actionable roadmap away from fossil fuel dependency, highlighting the influence of entrenched economic interests. While these shortcomings are disappointing, they offer a valuable opportunity for reflection and reform. The failure at COP31 should not be viewed as the collapse of the global climate effort but as an urgent signal that the status quo in multilateral climate negotiations is insufficient to meet the scale and immediacy of the crisis. This moment calls for re-energising international cooperation, urging countries to bridge their divergent interests and work with renewed transparency and solidarity. It also brings to light that the current voluntary pledging model needs firmer accountability mechanisms for enforcing compliance and incentivising larger, more actionable and ambitious commitments. The inability to get an overarching political consensus also demonstrates that countries are no longer willing to go along without assurance of financial, technical and policy support needed to adapt and recover. The setbacks also highlight the need to examine new approaches that include civil society, indigenous voices and private-sector leadership for fresh perspectives and urgency into a traditionally slow-moving process. The weak outcome at COP31 should not cause despair but create a renewed sense of purpose. Sometimes a failure in negotiations is less damaging than weak agreements (like previous COPs) that create a false sense of security. COP31 has forced a reset and serves as a crucial pivot point for rejecting unfair agreements and harnessing the moment to strengthen the spirit of the Paris Agreement, keeping its promise alive and escalating its ambition. The failure of COP31 is in fact a triumph of COP21. COP31 may have faltered but it reaffirmed the essential truth that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action. The diplomatic disagreements at COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 resulted in the milestone triumph of COP21 in 2015 in Paris. The failure of COP31 can serve the same turning-point purpose for future COPs and multilateralism. The writer is a climate policy analyst.aisha@csccc.org.pk

articles.title: Choking the provinces
articles.content: LET’S be very clear about one thing: this business of cutting theprovincesup into “administrative units” has nothing to do with good or bad governance. It is mainly about recentralising control over the state’s resources. A paper written by three eminent Pakistani academics in 2005 made a related point that is worth revisiting in the present debate. The authors were Ali Cheema, Asim Ijaz Khwaja and Adnan Qadir and the document was published in 2005 as a working paper for Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government. They took a longer view of all attempts to bring in local governments in the country’s history, and came to the following conclusion: “local government empowerment has always been combined with centralisation of political power in the hands of the non-representative centre. The centralisation of political power has undermined representative institutions not only at the level of the centre but also at the level of the provinces.” Their analysis is especially relevant all over again, as the same gambit to centralise power is being rolled out for the fourth time in our history. They noted that in all such experiments in the past, “[o]ur interpretation is that these reforms have been used as a means for a non-representative centre to gain legitimacy by by-passing the political agents at the provincial and national levels”. Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow. The seventh NFC award agreed to in 2009 and made effective in July 2010 reversed the centralisation of powers and resources that the federal authorities had grown accustomed to over the decades. It was the first time in Pakistan’s history that powers and, more importantly, resources, flowed down from the federal government towards lower tiers of government in such large quantities. And almost immediately, from its very first year of operation, a thrust emerged from the federal authorities to try and undo this. It began slowly at first. Then in the middle of the decade it achieved its first written form. Here is a brief timeline of how small, subtle changes in how fiscal resources are measured and counted turned into a full-blown programme for reversing the flow of these resources to the provincial governments. In FY2011, the first year after the seventh NFC award, the federal government “successfully pressed” the provincial governments to run a surplus and not spend all the money being devolved down to them. Then the next year they asked for these surpluses again, but with no Fund programme in force, the provincial governments did not comply. This changed in 2013 when the IMF made it a prior action for provinces to post a surplus, and provincial deposits with the State Bank leapt from Rs42 billion in June 2013 to Rs257bn by March 2014. This was ratified in the Council of Common Interests, and provincial finance secretaries agreed to continue the practice into 2015. By June 2015 the IMF programme called for written agreement from the provinces to raise their surpluses, as a prior action and a few months later, in September, provincial spending was capped at 6.5 per cent of GDP. By June 2016, as the programme was winding up with only a few months left in it, the government set up the Fiscal Coordination Committee to ensure that centre and provinces coordinate their spending and surpluses. The very next year, as the Fund programme ran out, provincial governments ramped up their spending, running a deficit of Rs163bn in FY17. In July 2019 another IMF programme was signed, after replacing finance ministers. This one again made it a prior action to get provinces to run surpluses, and raised the surplus targets from one to 2.7pc of GDP. That agreement was renewed in the two years that followed, and provincial surpluses leapt from Rs77bn in FY20 to Rs314bn in FY21 and Rs351bn in FY22. That was the most troubled programme of Pakistan’s history, with more false starts than any other programme Pakistan had ever signed. The blowout came in 2024. As part of the bailout in July 2023, the provinces now had to agree not only to post a surplus, but also submit spending plans. Provincial deposits were already netted against government borrowing in the IMF’s targets for the budget deficit and SBP’s net domestic assets, thereby helping the federal government meet its targets under the Fund programme. Most importantly, the targets for provincial surpluses agreed to in that programme rose to Rs1.2 trillion in the first year, rising to Rs1.9tn by FY27. So in 2011 the provinces left unspent 13.5pc of what they received as a transfer under the NFC award. This figure fell as soon as the Fund programme lapsed, then rose again every time Pakistan entered a Fund programme. Today it stands at 19pc, skyrocketing in the last three years. Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow. In May 2025, for example, provinces were required to put surplus cash into T-bills. Their holdings of federal government debt rose from Rs19bn in June 2025 to Rs1.8tn as of October 2026, though this figure fluctuates a lot with maturities every few months. And then in June 2026, under Article 164 grants, the provinces were made to hand over Rs1.0tn to the federal authorities, or about 12.66pc of each province’s NFC share. What began as a plea to restrain spending in 2011 slowly grew into a codified demand to run a surplus. Then the targets for these surpluses were raised. Then came requirements to buy government debt paper followed by a reverse flow from province to centre as a “grant” under Article 164. And now they want to dismantle the whole set-up altogether, in the name of governance. The irony here is that it is the governance failures of the federal authorities themselves that have fuelled their hunger for resources from the provincial authorities. The writer is a business and economy journalist.khurram.husain@gmail.comX:@khurramhusain

articles.title: Unchanged features
articles.content: “IF Cleopatra’s nose had been shorter,” the French philosopher Blaise Pascal once mused, “the whole face of the world would have been changed.” One wonders whether Indo-Pak relations might have been different, had Mrs Indira Gandhi’s nose been shorter. She was always self-conscious about it. In a letter to her American friend Dorothy Norman, Mrs Gandhi admitted: “Ever since plastic surgery was heard of, I have been wanting to get something done to my nose.” In 1967, she had the chance when, during an election rally, a projectile struck her directly in the face. Her son Rajiv recounted her concern later that “her already long nose would now be crooked too”. Perhaps the most memorable reference to her nose came from Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw, who, after the 1971 war, answered her fear that he might topple her in a military coup: “You see, you have a long nose, even I have a long nose, but that doesn’t mean I poke my nose in your business of running the country and you poke your long nose in my Army.” Mrs Gandhi never warmed to Pakistan. She never forgot Yahya Khan belittling her as “that woman”, nor forgave Z.A. Bhutto’s dismissal of her as “a mediocre woman with a mediocre intelligence [,] a diligent drudge of a schoolgirl [,] devoid of initiative and imagination”. Sonia Gandhi’s attitude towards Pakistan has hardened. She did not share her father Pandit Nehru’s sentiment about northwestern India. In his day, before 1947, he had travelled and canvassed there extensively. For example, writing to her from Lahore in August 1945, he described a tour from Nathiagali to Abbottabad, Haripur and Taxila, with a stop at the Mughal garden in Wah where he wanted to bathe in “the pool of wonderfully clear water”. In an earlier letter, written from Bareilly Central Prison, he reminisced: “I like going to Lahore [.] It is like a growing child, very immature in many ways, yet with an air of sophistication [.] However, there is an atmosphere of a fake and superficial gaiety”. If Pandit Nehru had been partly responsible for the first partition of India in August 1947 and his daughter Indira for the subsequent partition of Pakistan in December 1971, their successor Rajiv made a determined effort to bring his country and Pakistan closer. In her memoir Belonging (2026), Sonia Gandhi describes Rajiv’s conciliatory mission in 1989, the first visit by an Indian PM since his grandfather’s in 1960. Then, Nehru’s host had been a general, Ayub Khan. In 1989, Sonia recalls the freer atmosphere: “The air was full of excitement and expectation [.] Thirty-five-year-old Benazir Bhutto had recently been elected prime minister in Pakistan’s first democratic election since 1977, the first woman of the country to hold the post [.] Both Rajiv and Benazir had lost a cherished parent to political violence.” In time, both would be assassinated. Rajiv and Sonia, accompanied by their children Rahul and Priyanka, arrived in Islamabad on July 16, to be welcomed by Benazir and her husband Asif Zardari. The same evening, they had a private dinner with the couple. She recalled: “The atmosphere was informal, as we were young and found much in common”. However, “whenever the discussion veered towards political matters, our host [Benazir] would increase the volume of the music playing in the background, thereby warning us that people were listening in to our conversation”. Sonia was struck “by how much is recognisable between our ways and theirs: food, apparel, language, customs [.] We came away feeling that if only our two countries could sink their differences, how much both could benefit! Instead of armaments and wars, how much could be done for our people on both sides”. Gradually, Sonia’s attitude towards Pakistan hardened, as domestic imperatives made her relapse into an Indian stereotype. While she admired Nelson Mandela’s spirit of forgiveness, she found it impossible to follow his advice to convert “negative feelings” into “positivity and courage.” She allowed her PM Dr Manmohan Singh to improve Indo-Pak contacts, to promote a Lambah/Aziz backchannel, but fell short of allowing them to reach fruition. Today, PM Modi’s government has ensured that Pakistanis and Indians still need to go abroad to meet each other. (In 1989, Rajiv Gandhi regretted that as an alternative.) They know each other now only through ricocheted news and pirated editions. Will this current freeze ever defrost? It seems unlikely. Recently, Rahul Gandhi (now his mother’s successor as opposition leader), acknowledged that improved ties are possible, provided Pakistan eschews “cross-border terrorism”. Pakistan’s well-thumbed retort is first a resolution of the 78-year-old Jammu and Kashmir issue. The stance of each country, like Mrs Gandhi’s nose, remains an unchanged feature in the subcontinent’s politics. The writer is an author.www.fsaijazuddin.pk
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: New search trends
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S IT and software export story is told in remittance figures, freelancer rankings and new export targets. One question gets far less attention. When a buyer in Austin, Manchester or Dubai goes looking for a software vendor, where do they look now, and are Pakistani firms anywhere in the answer? For 20 years the answer was Google’s 10 blue links. Our software houses, Software as a Service (SaaS) start-ups and agencies learned that game: rank for the right phrases, get the click, win the call. Many still treat a page-one ranking as the finish line. The finish line has moved. My firm recently ran 1,500 real software-buying questions through four AI systems that buyers now use: ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Google’s AI Mode and the AI Overviews that sit at the top of ordinary Google results. We asked each question three times, from fresh sessions in the United States, and collected 18,000 answers across 20 software categories, from CRM and accounting to recruitment and e-signature tools. Three findings should worry anyone who sells Pakistani software or services abroad. Our IT exporters are optimising for a search page buyers no longer read. First, the AI answer is now the first thing a buyer sees. Google showed an AI Overview on 98 per cent of the software-buying searches we tested. The summary sits above the links, names a handful of products and often settles the question before anyone scrolls. A buyer can form a shortlist without visiting a single vendor website. Second, ranking on Google no longer guarantees a place in that summary. We looked at 27,307 websites cited inside AI Overviews. Only 28.1pc also ranked in the top three organic results on the same page. More striking, 36.5pc of the cited websites did not appear in the organic results shown at all. The AI is reading, and trusting, sources well beyond the page-one list our marketing teams obsess over. Third, the AI leans on what other people say about a product, not only on what the product says about itself. Review platforms such as G2, Capterra and TrustRadius were cited in 25.6pc of ChatGPT’s answers. Google’s AI Overviews cited YouTube in 80.5pc of answers and Reddit in 52.8pc. In plain terms, the machines are listening to reviews, videos and forum threads. Put those together and the problem for Pakistani exporters becomes clear. A firm can do everything right by the old rulebook, rank well and still be invisible when a foreign buyer asks an AI assistant for options. If that firm has no reviews on the platforms AI reads, no independent coverage and no presence in the conversations where buyers compare tools, the assistant simply has nothing to say about it. This matters more for us than for an American or European competitor. A Pakistani vendor already starts with a trust gap: unfamiliar brand, distant time zone, questions about payments and support. Third-party proof is how that gap gets closed. AI systems now automate the hunt for that proof. A buyer who would once have found us on page one may never hear our name. There is a fix, and none of it is exotic. Exporters should treat reviews as infrastructure, not vanity. Every satisfied foreign client is a potential review on a platform the AI reads. Many firms have satisfied foreign clients and few or no public reviews to show for them. That gap now costs visibility as well as credibility. They should earn mentions outside their own websites. Comparison articles, industry publications, podcasts, credible forum answers and expert commentary are now inputs to the AI shortlist. A website alone is not enough. They should measure the right thing. Ask the questions a real buyer would ask, in ChatGPT and Google, every month, and record whether your firm is named and how it is described. If you are not tracking that, you are not tracking where your next client is making up their mind. There is also a role for the industry bodies. P@SHA and the Pakistan Software Export Board already run trade delegations and export promotion. A modest programme to help member firms build verified review profiles, publish credible case studies and track their visibility in AI answers would do more for the “Brand Pakistan” tech story than another glossy brochure. The country’s export targets depend on buyers who have never met us. The first impression they get is increasingly written by a machine. None of this replaces good work. AI systems are not easily fooled for long, and what they repeat is mostly what credible people already say. But the rules of discovery have changed, and they have changed for everyone at once. That is rare, and it is an opening. Firms that adapt early can be named alongside global brands. Firms that wait will keep winning page-one rankings that fewer and fewer buyers ever see. The writer is founder and CEO of a search and AI visibility firm.
articles.author: Usman Tauqir

articles.title: Red lines
articles.content: INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi is right tosaythat freedom of expression cannot be a licence to promote terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence or child sexual exploitation. No responsible media outlet or citizen would argue otherwise. And few would object to curbing such content on social media. Those who spread such material should expect to answer for it under the law. But drawing red lines is only half the job. The state must also show that it respects them. This is where its record raises questions. There are visible red lines against hate and violence. But there are also invisible ones that journalists and citizens encounter every day when they question powerful quarters or report matters considered inconvenient. Journalists have been picked up, threatened and intimidated for publishing stories that upset those in power. Media organisations have faced pressure over their editorial choices. Reporters often find themselves working out what they can safely publish and which subjects are best avoided. This has created a vacuum that social media is rapidly filling. So when Mr Naqvi tells journalists they are free to report, and that citizens are free to ask questions, it rings hollow. Terms such as “anti-state activity”, “misinformation” and “hate speech” are elastic. And when officials interpret them without checks, they become tools for silencing critics. Having a law or a regulator does not make its use legitimate. Enforcement agencies should operate within defined legal limits, give valid and legitimate reasons for their decisions, act in proportion to the harm and be answerable to the courts. The rules should apply equally to everyone, whatever their politics or standing. Otherwise a measure meant to protect citizens ends up policing public debate. The minister’s assurance that dissent, including criticism of the state, will be heard is welcome. But assurances count for little while media organisations and journalists are still being intimidated. The state must guarantee complete press freedom, subject only to clearly defined constitutional and legal restrictions. A sensible first step would be to bring journalists and their representative bodies, media owners, civil society and relevant state institutions together to agree on what responsible expression means in practice. Such consultations should produce a clear commitment to protect journalists, safeguard editorial independence and prevent the misuse of regulatory powers. Freedom of expression carries responsibilities. But those responsibilities cannot be imposed on the media alone. The state must also accept its own obligations and allow uncomfortable questions to be asked. Rules against violence and hatred are fair enough. Unwritten and invisible ones against independent journalism are not.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Other realms
articles.content: IT was a moment of pride for Pakistan when PAF officer Muhammad Zeeshan Aliblasted offinto space yesterday morning alongside his Chinese colleagues, astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi. As the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft entered orbit soon after lift-off, Wing Commander Ali became Pakistan’sfirst orbital astronaut, carrying with him “the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis”. Three-and-a-half hours later, the Shenzhou-24 capsule docked with China’s Tiangongspace station, where the crew from an earlier mission warmly greeted the arriving astronauts — especially their first foreign guest. Wing Commander Ali, who has been designated a payload specialist, will spend about a week in space working on four experiments covering radiation protection, space food security, oxygen-producing microorganisms, and self-healing carbon fibres. With the successful launch of Shenzhou-24, Pakistan joins the ranks of around 50 countries that have sent their citizens into orbit. For years, China and Pakistan have worked closely in several sectors, ranging from defence and security to energy and infrastructure development under CPEC. As 2026 marks75 yearsof Pakistan-China diplomatic relations, it is only fitting that spaceflights should be the next sphere of cooperation. However, while a significant beginning has been made, it will be years before Pakistan can take the same strides in space technology as China. This moment of celebration must therefore give way to something more permanent — economic stability, greater investment in R&D, international collaborations in science and technology, and above all, a sound STEM education base. With a large youth population comes a strong talent pool. But governments here have left it untapped. Instead, they have given free rein toilliteracy, poverty, and poor schooling, closing many doors to opportunity. Contrast this reality with a space flight by one man from the same country that has brought hope to millions — a fleeting triumph that could acquire permanence if the state prioritised people’s welfare. “To every child who is watching while I am in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams,” was Zeeshan Ali’s message to youngsters as he set out to explore realms beyond Earth. Pakistan should not allow its children’s dreams to fade away.
articles.author: Editorial
